enzyme-catalysis-s1.title: Oxygen from hydrogen peroxide
enzyme-catalysis-s1.text: Catalase speeds the reaction 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. A student put 5 mL of 1.5% hydrogen peroxide in each of four flasks at 22 °C, added a different test material, and collected the oxygen gas in an upside-down graduated cylinder filled with water. If every hydrogen peroxide molecule in a flask broke down, about 27 mL of oxygen would be collected.

table.caption: Total oxygen collected (mL) after each time
cols: 0.1 g manganese dioxide powder (a non-living catalyst)

enzyme-catalysis-s2.title: Energy diagram for one reaction
enzyme-catalysis-s2.text: The graph shows the energy of the reacting molecules as a reaction proceeds from reactants (left) to products (right), with and without the enzyme that catalyzes it. Reaction progress has no units.

enzyme-catalysis-s3.title: Using the same enzyme six times
enzyme-catalysis-s3.text: Invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose. A company attached 2.0 mg of invertase to tiny plastic beads packed in a column. A fresh 100 mL batch of sucrose solution was poured through the column six times in a row, and the glucose leaving the column was measured each time. Afterward, the protein still attached to the beads was measured: 2.0 mg. 2.0 mg of invertase is about 7.4 × 10⁻⁹ mol of enzyme.

table.caption: Glucose produced by the column in each batch

items.q: What is the rate of oxygen production with fresh liver extract during the first 30 seconds, in mL per second? Give two decimal places.

why.correct: Rate = change in amount ÷ change in time = (9.0 mL − 0.0 mL) ÷ (30 s − 0 s) = 0.30 mL/s.

items.q: With fresh liver extract, oxygen production slows after 90 seconds and nearly stops by 180 seconds. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: Nearly all the hydrogen peroxide has been broken down, since the total is close to the 27 mL possible.
The catalase has been used up by the reaction, since each enzyme molecule can break down one hydrogen peroxide.
The oxygen produced has denatured the catalase, since the rate falls as more oxygen builds up in the flask.
The liver extract has run out of energy to give the reactants, since the rate drops steadily over time.

why.correct: 26.0 mL of a possible 27 mL has been collected, so the reactant is almost gone. With little hydrogen peroxide left, fewer molecules reach an active site each second.
options: The total collected nearly equals the maximum, which shows the reactant, not the enzyme, has run out.
Enzymes are not used up; each catalase molecule breaks down huge numbers of hydrogen peroxide molecules.
Nothing in the data tests oxygen's effect on the enzyme; the slowdown is explained by the reactant running out.
Enzymes do not supply energy to reactants; they lower the activation energy.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the flask with water instead of a catalyst?
options: It shows how much oxygen forms with no catalyst, the baseline the other flasks are compared with.
It shows that hydrogen peroxide breaks down quickly on its own, so a catalyst is not needed.
It replaces the boiled extract, so the experiment needs just one flask without a working catalyst.
It measures how much oxygen dissolves in water, which is then added to the other flasks' totals.

why.correct: With no catalyst, hydrogen peroxide still breaks down very slowly (0.9 mL in 180 s). That baseline shows how much each catalyst adds.
options: This flask gives the uncatalyzed rate, the reference point for every comparison.
Only 0.9 mL formed in 3 minutes, so breakdown on its own is very slow.
The boiled extract tests something different: whether the extract's effect needs a folded enzyme.
The water flask measures oxygen produced from hydrogen peroxide, not oxygen dissolving.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by comparing the manganese dioxide flask with the other flasks?
options: It speeds the reaction compared with water, though with these amounts more slowly at first than fresh extract.
Manganese dioxide is not a catalyst, because it is not a protein and has no active site to bind hydrogen peroxide.
Manganese dioxide and boiled extract work the same way, because both raised oxygen output above the water flask.
Manganese dioxide releases more energy from each hydrogen peroxide molecule than catalase does, so its rate keeps on rising longer.

why.correct: Manganese dioxide made 16.0 mL in 180 s, against 0.9 mL with water, so it catalyzes the reaction. Its first-30-s rate (0.10 mL/s) is a third of fresh extract's (0.30 mL/s) with the amounts used.
options: Both catalysts beat the water flask; fresh extract was faster at first with these amounts.
A catalyst is anything that speeds a reaction and is unchanged; non-living catalysts exist, and this one clearly sped the reaction.
Boiled extract (0.8 mL) did no better than water (0.9 mL), so it did not speed the reaction at all.
A catalyst does not change the energy a reaction releases; it changes only how fast the reaction goes.

items.q: At 180 seconds the student adds another 5 mL of 1.5% hydrogen peroxide to the fresh-extract flask. What is the most likely result?
options: Oxygen production speeds up again, well above its rate just before, because the catalase was not used up.
Oxygen production stays near zero, because the catalase was used up breaking the first 5 mL.
Oxygen production speeds up but stops after 0.2 mL, because each catalase molecule can act a few more times.
Oxygen production slows further, because adding more reactant dilutes the catalase in the flask.

why.correct: Catalase comes out of each reaction unchanged, so it can break down the new hydrogen peroxide and oxygen production jumps from almost nothing. It will not quite match the first 30 seconds, because the new peroxide is mixed into liquid already in the flask, so its concentration is lower than at the start.
options: The enzyme is reused; fresh reactant restarts the reaction at a similar rate.
Enzymes are not consumed, so the catalase still works after the first batch is gone.
Each catalase molecule can act millions of times; there is no small limit on uses.
The volume roughly doubles, which dilutes both catalase and peroxide somewhat, but the flask goes from almost no reactant to plenty, so the rate rises rather than falls.

items.q: What is the activation energy of the reaction without the enzyme, in kJ/mol?

why.correct: Activation energy = peak energy − energy of the reactants = 115 − 40 = 75 kJ/mol.

items.q: By what percentage does the enzyme lower the activation energy? Give a whole number.

why.correct: Without the enzyme: 115 − 40 = 75 kJ/mol. With it: 70 − 40 = 30 kJ/mol. Percent decrease = (75 − 30) ÷ 75 × 100 = 60%.

items.q: Based on the graph, how does the enzyme change the reaction?
options: It lowers the peak but leaves the reactant and product levels alone, so 25 kJ/mol is released either way.
It lowers the energy of the products, so the reaction releases more energy when the enzyme is present.
It raises the energy of the reactants so they start closer to the peak and need less energy to react.
It lowers both the energy peak and the product level by the same amount, so the energy released by the reaction is unchanged.

why.correct: Both curves start at 40 and end at 15 kJ/mol; only the peak differs (115 against 70). The energy released, 40 − 15 = 25 kJ/mol, is the same.
options: Same start, same end, lower peak: that is what an enzyme does.
Both curves end at 15 kJ/mol, so the products have the same energy with or without the enzyme.
Both curves start at 40 kJ/mol; the enzyme does not change the reactants' energy.
The product level is 15 kJ/mol on both curves; only the peak moves.

items.q: The same reaction can also run backward, from products to reactants. Using the graph, how does the enzyme affect the backward reaction?
options: It lowers its activation energy from 100 to 55 kJ/mol, so the enzyme speeds the backward reaction too.
It has no effect on it, because an enzyme's active site binds just the reactants of the forward reaction and not the products.
It lowers its activation energy from 75 to 30 kJ/mol, the same values as for the forward reaction.
It raises its activation energy, which is why the enzyme makes the reaction run in the forward direction.

why.correct: Going backward, the molecules start at the product level (15) and climb to the same peak: 115 − 15 = 100 kJ/mol without the enzyme, 70 − 15 = 55 with it. The enzyme lowers both barriers by 45 kJ/mol, so it speeds both directions.
options: The peak is shared by both directions, so lowering it lowers both barriers by the same 45 kJ/mol.
The backward reaction passes through the same transition state, which the enzyme stabilizes; the graph shows the lower peak serves both directions.
Those values are measured from the reactant level (40); the backward reaction starts at the product level (15).
The peak is lower with the enzyme, so the climb from the products is smaller, not larger.

items.q: What does the highest point on each curve represent?
options: The transition state, the least stable arrangement on the path
The moment the products are released from the enzyme's active site
The energy the enzyme adds to the reactants to start the reaction
The total energy stored in the products once the reaction is finished

why.correct: The peak is the transition state: bonds partly broken and partly formed, the highest-energy, least stable point on the path.
options: The top of the hill is the transition state, between reactants and products.
Products appear on the right side of the graph, after the peak, at 15 kJ/mol.
The enzyme adds no energy; the curve with the enzyme is lower, not higher.
The products' energy is the flat level on the right (15 kJ/mol), not the peak.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: Output stayed between 4.6 and 4.8 mmol per batch, with no steady decline.
Glucose output fell by about half between the first batch and the sixth batch.
Output rose with each batch as the enzyme got better at binding sucrose.
Glucose output was highest in the last batch and lowest in the first batch.

why.correct: All six batches gave 4.6-4.8 mmol, and the values move up and down rather than falling steadily.
options: The range is narrow (4.6-4.8 mmol) with no downward trend.
Batch 6 (4.7 mmol) is almost the same as batch 1 (4.8 mmol), not half.
Output did not rise, and enzymes do not learn; each binding is a separate event.
Batch 1 (4.8) was among the highest and batch 6 (4.7) was not the highest.

items.q: Which conclusion do the data most directly support?
options: Invertase is not used up: the same enzyme molecules kept making glucose batch after batch.
Invertase lowers the activation energy of sucrose breakdown by about 4.8 kJ/mol in each batch.
Invertase becomes part of the glucose it makes, so the beads lose some enzyme with each batch.
Invertase acts on sucrose but not on other sugars, since glucose came out of each of the six batches.

why.correct: Output stayed steady over six batches, and the beads still held 2.0 mg of enzyme at the end. The enzyme was reused, not consumed.
options: Steady output and unchanged enzyme mass both show the enzyme was reused.
The 4.8 values are amounts of glucose in mmol, not energies; the setup measures no energy.
The beads held 2.0 mg before and after, so no enzyme was lost into the product.
Only sucrose was tested, so the data say nothing about other sugars.

items.q: How much glucose, in mmol, did the column produce over all six batches? Give one decimal place.
About how many glucose molecules did each invertase molecule produce over the six batches? (28.4 mmol = 2.84 × 10⁻² mol.)
options: About 4 million (4 × 10⁶)
About 4 thousand (4 × 10³)
About 1
About 4 billion (4 × 10⁹)

why.correct: Glucose per enzyme = moles of glucose ÷ moles of enzyme = (2.84 × 10⁻² mol) ÷ (7.4 × 10⁻⁹ mol) ≈ 3.8 × 10⁶, about 4 million.
options: 2.84 × 10⁻² ÷ 7.4 × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 3.8 × 10⁶: millions of reactions per enzyme molecule.
This uses millimoles of glucose (28.4) against micromoles of enzyme; convert both to moles first.
One product per enzyme would mean the enzyme is used up; the steady output shows it is not.
This is a thousand times too high; check the powers of ten when dividing.

items.q: What is activation energy?
options: The energy reactants need to reach the transition state before becoming products
The energy a reaction releases as its reactants are turned into products
The energy that an enzyme adds to its substrate so that the substrate is able to react
The energy stored in the bonds of the products once the reaction is complete

why.correct: Activation energy is the climb from the reactants up to the transition state, the energy barrier every reaction must clear.
options: This is the definition: the barrier between reactants and the transition state.
That is the difference between reactants and products, which an enzyme does not change.
Enzymes add no energy; they lower the barrier.
The products' energy is the end level of the diagram, not the barrier.

items.q: Breaking sucrose into glucose and fructose releases energy, yet a bowl of table sugar stays sucrose for years. Which explanation is best?
options: Its activation energy is high, so at room temperature almost no sucrose reaches the transition state.
The reaction absorbs energy overall, so it happens just when energy is supplied from outside.
Sucrose is a product of this reaction, not a reactant, so the reaction is unable to start.
The glucose and fructose re-form sucrose as fast as it breaks, so the amount of sucrose looks constant.

why.correct: Whether a reaction releases energy and how fast it runs are different questions. A high activation energy keeps this reaction extremely slow, even though it releases energy, without a catalyst.
options: A high barrier makes the reaction slow even though it releases energy overall.
The stem says the reaction releases energy; what stops it is the barrier, not the overall energy change.
Sucrose is the reactant here; it is broken into glucose and fructose.
No glucose or fructose is forming in the bowl in measurable amounts, so there is nothing to re-form sucrose.

items.q: Both heating a reaction and adding an enzyme make it go faster. How do the two differ?
options: Heating gives more molecules enough energy to clear the same barrier; an enzyme lowers the barrier.
Heating lowers the activation energy, while an enzyme gives the substrate the extra energy it needs to react.
Heating changes which products the reaction makes, while an enzyme keeps the products the same.
Heating works for reactions that release energy overall, while an enzyme works for reactions that absorb it.

why.correct: Higher temperature means faster molecules, so a bigger share has enough energy to reach the transition state. An enzyme changes the path so less energy is needed.
options: Heat changes the molecules' energy; the enzyme changes the height of the hill.
This reverses the two: heating supplies energy; enzymes lower the barrier and supply none.
Neither heating nor an enzyme changes which products a given reaction makes.
Both can speed either kind of reaction; neither choice depends on whether energy is released.

items.q: A student measures the product of an enzyme reaction every minute: 0, 12, 22, 29, 33 and 35 µmol at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 minutes. Which statement best describes the reaction rate?
options: It is highest in the first minute (12 µmol/min) and falls as substrate is used up.
It is constant at 7 µmol/min, the total product divided by the total time.
It rises each minute, because the amount of product goes up each minute.
It is highest in the last minute, when the most product is present in the tube.

why.correct: Product added per minute: 12, 10, 7, 4, 2 µmol. The rate, the slope, is steepest at the start and falls as the remaining substrate drops.
options: The per-minute gains fall from 12 to 2 µmol, so the rate is highest at first.
35 ÷ 5 = 7 is the average rate; the actual rate changes from 12 down to 2 µmol/min.
The amount of product rises, but the amount added each minute (the rate) falls.
The last minute added only 2 µmol, the smallest gain; rate is the change per minute, not the total.

items.q: Select the three ways an active site can lower the activation energy of a reaction.
options: Holding two reactants close together in the orientation in which they react
Bending or straining bonds of the substrate toward the shape of the transition state
Placing charged or polar side chains next to the bonds that change
Transferring heat from the enzyme to the substrate so it moves faster
Lowering the energy of the products so more energy is released
Adding energy from the enzyme's own bonds, which break as the reaction runs

why.correct: Active sites bring reactants together in the right orientation, strain the substrate toward the transition state, and provide side chains whose charges or polar groups help bonds break and form.
options: Correct orientation means fewer chance meetings are wasted.
Strain pushes the substrate partway toward the transition state.
Charged and polar side chains can give or take hydrogen ions or stabilize charges as bonds change.
Enzymes do not heat their substrates; they change the path, not the temperature.
The products' energy is the same with or without the enzyme.
The enzyme comes out unchanged, so it cannot be spending its own bonds.

items.q: An enzyme is added to a tube in which a slow reaction that releases energy is running at 25 °C. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Activation energy of the reaction
variables.why: The enzyme's active site makes the transition state easier to reach, lowering the barrier.

variables.name: Energy released per mole of reactant that reacts
variables.why: The reactants and products have the same energy with or without the enzyme, so the energy released is unchanged.

variables.name: Time needed to make 1 mmol of product
variables.why: A lower barrier means more molecules react per second, so the same amount of product forms sooner.

variables.name: Amount of enzyme in the tube after 1 hour
variables.why: Enzymes are not used up; after releasing the products each enzyme molecule has its original structure.

why.correct: An enzyme lowers the activation energy and so raises the rate. It changes neither the energy released nor its own amount.

items.q: A student claims that enzymes make reactions happen that would never occur without them. Which reasoning best evaluates the claim?
options: Wrong: an enzyme speeds a reaction that can already occur and does not change whether it releases energy.
Right: without an enzyme the activation energy of a reaction is infinite, so the reaction has no way to start.
Right: an enzyme provides the energy that an energy-absorbing reaction lacks, so the reaction can go.
Wrong: enzymes change which products form, so they create new reactions instead of speeding old ones.

why.correct: Enzymes change the path, not the start and end points. A reaction that does not happen on its own because it would need an energy input still needs that input with an enzyme; one that can happen just happens faster.
options: Enzymes change speed only; the reactants, products and overall energy change are fixed.
Uncatalyzed reactions have a finite barrier; the water flask in a catalase experiment still makes a little oxygen.
Enzymes supply no energy; reactions that need energy get it by being linked to other reactions, a topic for 3.4.
The products of a reaction are the same with or without the enzyme.
